hints: Start by identifying the two elements present in $\text{NaN}_3$ and the simple substances they form as products, $\text{Na}$ and $\text{N}_2$.
walkthrough:
Spot what decomposes into what**
You have sodium azide, $\text{NaN}_3$, breaking down into its elements. That means the only products can be sodium metal, $\text{Na}$, and nitrogen gas, $\text{N}_2$. Remember nitrogen exists as diatomic molecules, not single $\text{N}$ atoms.

Balance the nitrogen atoms**
One $\text{NaN}_3$ gives three $\text{N}$ atoms, but $\text{N}_2$ needs them in pairs. The smallest numbers that work are $2\text{NaN}_3 \rightarrow 2\text{Na} + 3\text{N}_2$. Check: 2 Na and 6 N on both sides, so it balances.

hints: Count the total valence electrons to share: 5 from each N plus 1 extra for the 1- charge, giving 16 electrons in total.
Think of a linear $\text{N-N-N}$ arrangement where the central N must share all its electrons in multiple bonds so that every N ends with an octet.
Recall that one end N will need three lone pairs and the other end N will need two lone pairs to complete octets, with the whole diagram in square brackets with a 1- charge.
walkthrough:
Count the electrons you must show**
Each N is in Group 15 so brings 5 outer electrons. Three Ns give 15, plus one extra electron for the 1- charge shown as $\Box$. Total is 16 valence electrons. Use $\bullet$ for the 5 electrons from the central N, $\times$ for the 10 electrons from the two outer Ns, and $\Box$ for the added electron.

Build octets with multiple bonds**
Place the three Ns in a line. To give every N 8 electrons with only 16 electrons total, the central N must form four bonds in total. A common form is $[\text{N} \equiv \text{N}^{+}-\text{N}^{2-}]$ or the two double bond resonance form. That means the central N has 8 shared electrons and no lone pair.

Finish the outer Ns and add the charge**
Give each outer N its lone pairs so each has 8: one terminal N has one lone pair plus a triple bond (8 electrons), the other has three lone pairs plus a single bond (8 electrons). Put large square brackets around the whole $\text{N}_3$ unit and write $-$ outside to show the overall $\text{N}_3^-$ charge.

Final answer: Linear $\text{N-N-N}$ ion with 16 valence electrons shown. Central N has 8 electrons in its outer shell with no lone pair, each outer N has 8 electrons including lone pairs. One $\text{N-N}$ is triple bond, other is single or double bond (resonance forms with 4 shared pairs in total), enclosed in [ ] with $-$ charge.

hints: Focus on the direction for lattice formation: start from separated gaseous ions and end with one mole of solid lattice.
Remember the two precise definition details: amount is 1 mole and conditions are standard conditions (298 K, 100 kPa).
walkthrough:
Picture ions coming together**
Lattice energy is about forming the giant ionic lattice. Imagine $\text{Na}^{+}(\text{g})$ and $\text{N}_3^{-}(\text{g})$ far apart in the gas phase, then they pack together to make $\text{NaN}_3(\text{s})$. The equation is $\text{Na}^{+}(\text{g}) + \text{N}_3^{-}(\text{g}) \rightarrow \text{NaN}_3(\text{s})$.

Add the exact definition conditions**
For full marks you must state amount and conditions. It is the enthalpy change when 1 mole of the solid is formed, and the ions start as gases under standard conditions. That precision is what separates a vague answer from a Cambridge definition.
Final answer: Enthalpy change when 1 mole of solid ionic compound is formed from its gaseous ions under standard conditions.

hints: Think about what happens in terms of attraction when oppositely charged gaseous ions come together to make bonds.
walkthrough:
Link attraction to energy release**
When $\text{Na}^{+}$ and $\text{N}_3^{-}$ approach, there is strong electrostatic attraction between opposite charges. Making bonds or attractions always releases energy to the surroundings, so the process is exothermic and $\Delta H_{latt}^{\ominus}$ is always negative.
Final answer: Lattice formation involves bond making / electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions which releases energy, so $\Delta H$ is negative.

hints: Draw a Born-Haber cycle for $\text{NaN}_3$: formation goes via atomisation of Na, first ionisation of Na, formation of $\text{N}_3^-(\text{g})$, then lattice formation.

Find the missing first ionisation energy of Na from the Data Booklet, $+496 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$, and set up $\Delta H_f^{\ominus} = \Delta H_{at}^{\ominus} + IE + \Delta H(\text{N}_3^-) + \Delta H_{latt}^{\ominus}$.
Substitute the signs carefully: $+107 +496 +142 -732$ and check whether the final answer should be small and positive.
walkthrough:
Write the Hess law route**
To make $\text{NaN}_3(\text{s})$ from elements, go the long way round: $\text{Na}(\text{s}) \rightarrow \text{Na}(\text{g})$ atomisation $+107$, $\text{Na}(\text{g}) \rightarrow \text{Na}^{+}(\text{g}) + e^-$ ionisation, $1\frac{1}{2}\text{N}_2(\text{g}) + e^- \rightarrow \text{N}_3^-(\text{g})$ given as $+142$, then $\text{Na}^{+}(\text{g}) + \text{N}_3^-(\text{g}) \rightarrow \text{NaN}_3(\text{s})$ lattice $-732$. By Hess law, $\Delta H_f^{\ominus}$ is the sum of these steps.

Pull the ionisation energy from the Data Booklet**
The question gives you all data except $IE_1(\text{Na})$. From the Data Booklet this is $+496 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$. Do not guess it, this is a classic Paper 4 skill of combining given data with Booklet data.

Substitute with signs and calculate**
$$\Delta H_f^{\ominus} = 107 + 496 + 142 - 732$$
Add the endothermic steps: $107 + 496 + 142 = +745$. Then add the exothermic lattice step: $745 - 732 = +13$. So $\Delta H_f^{\ominus} = +13 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ including the positive sign.

Final answer: $$\Delta H_f^{\ominus} = \Delta H_{at}^{\ominus}(\text{Na}) + IE(\text{Na}) + \Delta H^{\ominus}(\text{N}_3^-) + \Delta H_{latt}^{\ominus}$$
$$= 107 + 496 + 142 - 732 = +13 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$

hints: Compare the sizes of the cations $\text{Na}^{+}$ and $\text{Rb}^{+}$ down Group 1 and think how ionic radius affects attraction to the same anion.
walkthrough:
Use ionic size to explain attraction strength**
Both compounds contain the same $\text{N}_3^-$ anion with 1+ cations, so charge is identical. The difference is size: $\text{Na}^{+}$ is much smaller than $\text{Rb}^{+}$ because Rb is further down Group 1 with more shells. Smaller ions get closer together, so electrostatic attraction between $\text{Na}^{+}$ and $\text{N}_3^-$ is stronger, more energy is released on lattice formation, making $\Delta H_{latt}^{\ominus}$ more negative.
Final answer: $\text{Na}^{+}$ is smaller than $\text{Rb}^{+}$ so there is stronger electrostatic attraction to the $\text{N}_3^-$ ion, giving a more exothermic lattice energy.
